recommended.name: Golden Delicious
recommended.use: fresh eating, cooking (partially self-fruitful; universal pollinizer)
recommended.recommended_note: Near-universal pollinizer: heavy, long bloom and viable pollen make it a reliable partner for almost any other apple variety. Partially self-fruitful, but still crops better with a cross.

from.note_seasoned: Thirteen cultivars sequenced very early to very late by bloom so you can pair overlapping bloom groups for cross-pollination. Chill need spans roughly 100 hours (Dorsett Golden, Ein Shemer, Anna) to about 900 hours (McIntosh): match it to your winters. Liberty is scab-resistant and a low-spray pick for humid regions; Golden Delicious is a near-universal pollinizer; Honeycrisp, Fuji, Granny Smith, and Pink Lady store well.
from.note_beginner: Pick at least two different varieties that bloom around the same time so they can pollinate each other. If you garden where winters are mild, choose low-chill kinds like Dorsett Golden, Anna, or Ein Shemer. If summers are humid and you want less spraying, Liberty resists apple scab. Golden Delicious is a great all-around partner that pollinates almost any other apple.

recommended.name: Dorsett Golden
recommended.note_beginner: A low-chill apple bred for mild-winter gardens, sweet and good for fresh eating, ripening early. It pollinates Anna, and University of Arizona Extension reports it cropping well in the low desert.
recommended.note_seasoned: Low-chill dessert apple; University of Arizona reports it cropping in the low desert around 100 chill hours, though stated lab requirements run higher (Texas A&M 350, UF/IFAS 250 to 300). Very early bloom, early ripening, a reliable pollinizer for Anna.

recommended.name: Anna
recommended.note_beginner: One of the best apples for warm-winter regions, crisp and sweet, ripening very early. Plant it near Dorsett Golden so the two pollinate each other; it crops well in the low desert.
recommended.note_seasoned: Low-chill cultivar, about 200 chill hours as reported cropping in the Arizona low desert (stated lab figures run higher, 250 to 400). Very early bloom, early ripening; pair with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer.

recommended.name: Ein Shemer
recommended.note_beginner: A low-chill yellow apple for mild winters, good fresh or cooked, ripening in mid-summer. It sets some fruit on its own but does better with a partner, and it crops in the low desert.
recommended.note_seasoned: Low-chill cultivar, around 100 chill hours per Arizona low-desert cropping reports (UF/IFAS states 450 as a lab requirement). Very early bloom, mid-season ripening; partially self-fruitful.

recommended.name: Zestar!
recommended.note_beginner: An early-season eating apple from Minnesota, crisp and sweet-tart, ripening in late summer. It is very cold hardy, so winter chill is never the limiting factor where it grows.
recommended.note_seasoned: Cold-hardy UMN release, very early bloom, early (late-August) ripening. No chill-hour figure is established in the literature; chill is not limiting in its cold-climate range, so the value here is a placeholder.

recommended.name: McIntosh
recommended.note_beginner: The classic tart, aromatic New England apple for fresh eating and sauce, ripening mid-season. It wants a good stretch of winter cold, so it suits colder regions.
recommended.note_seasoned: High-chill heirloom (nursery estimate near 900 hours), early-to-mid bloom, mid-season ripening. Tender flesh, excellent for sauce.

recommended.name: Liberty
recommended.note_beginner: A disease-resistant apple that shrugs off apple scab, so it is a great low-spray choice, good fresh, ripening mid to late season. A Cornell release built for easy backyard growing.
recommended.note_seasoned: Scab-immune Cornell cultivar, early bloom, ripe about ten days after McIntosh. Nursery chill estimate near 800 hours; a low-spray standout.
recommended.disease_notes: Immune to apple scab; a strong low-spray choice.

recommended.name: Empire
recommended.note_beginner: A sweet, crisp McIntosh-type apple for fresh eating that ripens in early fall and stores well. It can set some fruit on its own but crops better with a partner nearby.
recommended.note_seasoned: McIntosh x Red Delicious, mid bloom, late ripening. Listed as partially self-fruitful (Missouri G6001) but sets more when cross-pollinated; nursery chill estimate 600 to 800 hours.

recommended.name: Honeycrisp
recommended.note_beginner: The famously crisp, juicy snacking apple, ripening mid-season. It needs a different variety blooming at the same time to pollinate it.
recommended.note_seasoned: UMN release, mid-season bloom (Utah State labels it early; we keep the common mid classification), mid ripening. Needs a pollinizer; nursery chill estimate 800 to 1000 hours.

recommended.name: Gala
recommended.note_beginner: A mild, sweet, reliable apple for fresh eating, ripening in September, and one of the most popular apples grown. It sets some fruit alone but does best with a partner.
recommended.note_seasoned: Mid bloom, mid ripening, about 600 chill hours (Texas A&M). Shows some self-fertility but crops better cross-pollinated; pairs well with Honeycrisp.

recommended.name: Golden Delicious
recommended.note_beginner: A sweet, all-purpose yellow apple that is also the most useful partner in the orchard: it pollinates almost any other apple. Good fresh or cooked, ripening late in the season.
recommended.note_seasoned: Near-universal pollinizer, partially self-fruitful (semi-self-pollinating per Utah State), mid bloom, late ripening. Chill figure is uncertain (nursery sources range 700 to 1500), so treat it as approximate; note it can be ineffective as a pollinizer for Mutsu.

recommended.name: Jonagold
recommended.note_beginner: A large, honeyed, crisp apple that is wonderful fresh, ripening late in the season. Important catch: it cannot pollinate other trees, so it needs two other varieties nearby to fruit well.
recommended.note_seasoned: Triploid (sterile pollen), confirmed by NC State, Maine, and Missouri Extension; needs two non-triploid pollinizers. Mid bloom, late ripening; nursery chill estimate 700 to 800 hours.

recommended.name: Mutsu
recommended.note_beginner: A big, crisp, slightly tart green-gold apple (also sold as Crispin), great fresh or cooked, ripening late. Like Jonagold it cannot pollinate others and needs two partners of its own.
recommended.note_seasoned: Triploid (sterile pollen), about 600 chill hours (Texas A&M). Mid bloom, late ripening; needs two non-triploid pollinizers, and Golden Delicious is not a reliable one for it.

recommended.name: Fuji
recommended.note_beginner: A very sweet, dense, long-keeping apple for fresh eating, ripening late in the season, and one of the most widely grown apples. It needs a pollinizer blooming at the same time.
recommended.note_seasoned: Late bloom, late ripening, about 600 chill hours (Texas A&M; UF/IFAS 575). Self-sterile; stores exceptionally well.

recommended.name: Granny Smith
recommended.note_beginner: The tart bright-green cooking and eating apple, ripening very late in the season. A useful point: it blooms in mid-season even though it ripens late, so it can pollinate the mid-season apples.
recommended.note_seasoned: Mid bloom but late ripening (the bloom/ripen split matters for pairing), about 600 chill hours (UF/IFAS). Listed as partially self-fruitful; needs a long warm season to finish.

recommended.name: Pink Lady
recommended.note_beginner: A crisp, tangy-sweet pink apple that ripens the latest of all and stores for months. Like Granny Smith it blooms mid-season, so it can partner the mid-season apples even though its fruit finishes last.
recommended.note_seasoned: Cripps Pink; mid bloom, very late ripening (harvest October and later), 500 to 600 chill hours (Texas A&M). Self-sterile; the longest season of the set.

recommended.name: Dolgo
recommended.note_beginner: A flowering crabapple that blooms early and for a long time, which makes it a near-universal pollinizer for a whole row of apples. Its small tart fruit is good for jelly, and it can set fruit on its own.
recommended.note_seasoned: Long, early bloom spanning several apple groups, so it pollinizes across early-to-mid varieties; self-fertile. Nursery chill estimate about 500 hours; ploidy is not confirmed in a citable source but it is used horticulturally as a fertile pollinizer.

value.note_seasoned: Sixteen cultivars, thirteen dessert and cooking apples plus two triploids (Jonagold, Mutsu) and the Dolgo crabapple pollinizer, with bloom group kept distinct from ripening season. Pair overlapping bloom groups for cross-pollination; the triploids carry sterile pollen and need two non-triploid partners. Bloom group, ripening, and pollination are anchored to extension sources (Utah State, Missouri G6001, Texas A&M, UF/IFAS, NC State, Maine). Chill-hour data is thinner: extension figures exist mainly for warm-climate varieties where chill is limiting, so several cold-climate cultivars carry nursery estimates and Zestar! has none established. Chill requirement is model-dependent and shifts with local climate; read the per-variety confidence tier as the honest measure of each figure.
value.note_beginner: Plant at least two different varieties that bloom around the same time so they can pollinate each other. Where winters are mild, choose low-chill kinds like Dorsett Golden, Anna, or Ein Shemer. If summers are humid and you want to spray less, Liberty resists apple scab. Golden Delicious pollinates almost anything and makes a reliable partner, and a Dolgo crabapple blooms early and long enough to pollinate a whole row. Two varieties here, Jonagold and Mutsu, cannot pollinate anything and need two other partners themselves. One honest note on the numbers: bloom times, ripening, and pollination come from university extension guides and are solid, but chill hours (the winter cold a tree needs to fruit) are well documented only for warm-climate apples, so several cold-climate varieties here carry nursery estimates and a few newer ones like Zestar! have no firm figure yet. Treat the chill numbers as a guide, and check each variety's confidence tier to see how sure we are.
